input.content:
## Plain English

The `site_visits` table had two identical filing systems for the same piece of data — both were sorting rows by professional and time in exactly the same way. Every time a new visit was recorded, the database had to update both, but when looking data up it only ever used one. We removed the redundant duplicate, so each visit is now filed once instead of twice — faster writes, less storage used, no change to how queries work.

## Technical Summary

Created `supabase/migrations/20260509200000_drop_duplicate_site_visits_index.sql` with a single `DROP INDEX IF EXISTS analytics.site_visits_professional_time_idx`. This removes the index that was identical to `analytics_site_visits_professional_occurred_idx` (both covered `(professional_id, occurred_at)` ASC with no INCLUDE clause). The third index `site_visits_pro_date_range_idx` — which has `DESC` ordering plus `INCLUDE (country_code, device_type)` — was left untouched as it is functionally distinct. No PHP app code referenced either index name by string; grep confirmed clean across the entire `app/` directory.

## Decisions Made

- **Which index to keep**: Kept `analytics_site_visits_professional_occurred_idx` over `site_visits_professional_time_idx` because its name follows the `analytics_<table>_<cols>_idx` convention used by surrounding indexes in the baseline migration.
- **Migration timestamp**: Used `20260509200000` (next available slot after `20260509100000_drop_custom_domain.sql`).

## Notes

The two test failures seen in `composer test` (`Brand\OpenInviteTest`) are pre-existing and caused by a missing S3 bucket environment variable — entirely unrelated to this schema-only migration. Supabase migrations do not participate in the SQLite in-memory test suite.
